title: Thy people shall be my people (Ruth 1:16–17)
word: Thy people shall be my people
hook: Ruth clings to Naomi: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naomi at the gate of Bethlehem asked to be called Mara. Your line was stay beside them, let their words stand. Whose hard words did you let stand? Today, we step back onto the road, before the gate, to hear what Ruth said. Day eight hundred thirty-five.
screen: `STAY BESIDE THEM, LET THEIR WORDS STAND.`

segments.voice: On the road out of Moab, Naomi keeps sending her daughters-in-law home, and her argument is practical, almost brutal. I'm too old to have a husband. Even if I had sons tonight, would you wait for them to grow up? Go back. Orpah weeps, kisses her, and turns for home, and the book never blames her. Ruth doesn't move. So Naomi points down the road at the figure getting smaller. In the King James: "Behold, thy sister in law is gone back unto her people, and unto her gods: return thou after thy sister in law." It's the last door Naomi can open for her. And Ruth closes it.
screen: `GO BACK, I HAVE NOTHING TO GIVE.` → `ORPAH TURNS FOR HOME.` → `RETURN THOU AFTER THY SISTER.`

segments.voice: Ruth's answer holds the line in today's title: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Today, listen to how it ends. "Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried: the LORD do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me." Three things are packed in there. First, she goes past a lifetime. Not just I'll come with you, but I'll be buried where you're buried. Not even her bones are going back to Moab. Second, she seals it with an oath, and she swears by the LORD, the name of Naomi's God. A woman of Moab, on a road out of Moab, binds herself in the name she's choosing. Third, and this is easy to miss, look at what Naomi does. "When she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her." That's all. No embrace in the text. No thank you. Naomi just stops arguing, and they walk on, and the next thing she says out loud, at the gate, is that she came home empty. Ruth's loyalty isn't thanked on the spot. It doesn't need to be. The rabbis heard even more in these lines. In the Talmud, in tractate Yevamot, they imagine a whole conversation hidden in the speech: Naomi naming, one by one, what this life will ask of her, and each of Ruth's phrases answering, I accept. And some readers find one word under all of it, a word Ruth never says but lives out: chesed, loyal kindness that keeps going after it's been told to stop.
screen: `PAST A LIFETIME, TO THE GRAVE.` · `SHE SWEARS BY NAOMI'S GOD.` · then, large: `THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.` · then: `NAOMI SAYS NOTHING, AND THEY WALK ON.`

segments.voice: Today, the practice is to stay loyal to someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is hard to stay with right now. Not someone who harms you; someone who is grieving, prickly, distant, or just not saying thank you. A parent, a friend, a sibling, a neighbor. Walk beside them in your mind, on a long road, with nothing being said. Ask what staying would look like this week: a call you keep making, a visit, a seat saved, a message that asks for nothing back. Choose one. If you pray, you can say their name to God as you walk. The bell holds the time.
Thy people shall be my people. Ruth's vow on the road to Naomi, sealed by an oath that only death will part them. Today's word.
screen: `THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: thy people, my people. Today, stay loyal in one small way nobody will thank you for, and keep walking anyway. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Jews read Ruth's vow in the book of Ruth on Shavuot, and Jewish tradition looks to Ruth as the example of someone who joins the Jewish people by choice.

fork.setup: you're Naomi. Ruth has just sworn to live where you live and be buried where you're buried. what do you do?
options: thank her and hold her close.
keep arguing until she goes home.
fork.reveal: "when she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her." no thanks in the text, just silence, and the road.

original.note: Hebrew: "thy people, my people," two words in Ruth 1:16.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet line for a wedding card.
what it means: a vow to the grave, said to a grieving mother-in-law who answers with silence.
what a scholar hears: an oath sworn by the LORD's name, and the Talmud's reading in Yevamot of a hidden dialogue inside the speech.
